findings.title: Equal-priority crypto providers are now selected by classpath order
findings.body: All built-in server providers return the same priority (200): DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, and FIPS1402Provider. This sort has no tie handling, so if more than one is present the selected provider is whichever ServiceLoader resource happens to be encountered first. Previously this configuration failed closed; now, for example, a deployment containing both the default and FIPS providers can silently select the non-FIPS provider. The collection also instantiates every provider before choosing one, so ignored providers still execute constructor side effects such as Java security-provider registration. Reject equal highest priorities (or define an explicit safe policy) rather than continuing with an arbitrary provider.

findings.title: Adding an abstract SPI method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: CryptoProvider is a public ServiceLoader SPI, and making order() abstract is binary- and source-incompatible with implementations built against the previous interface. Existing provider jars will load but throw AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration sorts them and invokes order(), preventing application startup; source implementations no longer compile either. Provide a default order() implementation so existing providers remain usable, while allowing new implementations to override it.

findings.title: ECDSA conversion accepts signatures with trailing bytes
findings.body: concatenatedRSToASN1DER copies only the first signLength bytes and never checks signature.length. A fixed-width ECDSA JOSE R||S value with a valid signLength-byte prefix plus arbitrary trailing bytes is therefore converted to the same DER value as the original signature and can verify successfully. Conversely, short input produces an unchecked array-copy exception instead of a controlled invalid-signature result. Validate that signLength is valid and signature.length is exactly signLength before splitting R and S.

findings.title: ES384 and ES512 tests do not use their required EC curves
findings.body: The test creates one uninitialized EC KeyPairGenerator and reuses its default key pair for ES256, ES384, and ES512. On typical JDKs that is a P-256 key, so the ES384 and ES512 cases do not exercise P-384 and P-521 component sizes; in particular ES512 never exercises the long-form DER sequence length and 66-byte scalar handling expected for P-521. Generate keys explicitly with the curve corresponding to each algorithm and verify that the regenerated DER signature validates with the public key.
